doc.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025

title: Bitches Brew sessions and Teo Macero
summary: He says he was prepared for Miles's music; Bitches Brew was a jam with interludes, assembled by Macero, with Miles apart in his own spot.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: I was happy to see — I have the whole collection of Marian McPartland’s “Piano Jazz” and you did a session with her.
And there’s a quote in here from you, “I got around so well on Miles’ music because I like the unexpected.” Was “Bitches Brew” an unexpected situation for you or had you been sort of set up for that?

Yeah I was set up and prepared. I’m from Chicago, where I played various kinds of music. So I didn’t have any biases toward all the so-called genres of music. You know “Bitches Brew” was basically kind of a jam session with — not highly arranged, but with, you know, melodic interludes in between things. And then Miles let the tapes roll and got a groove that he liked and then he would play or somebody — Bennie Maupin would play, different players would solo on top of that. And then through Teo Macero,
his producer, through his artistry of putting all the different tracks together to tell a story, he did that very well.
I’m trying to picture you and the other musicians, the first time you heard the final product. Did you like it?
Yeah. That’s what I meant by Teo. Teo put the sequence together in a way that told a story.
Don Alias had something to say about the session that was kind of similar. I assume that you were sort of in a circle around miles logistically? Is that how that worked?
Miles had his own place with a speaker so he could hear everything.
